x.ASV: He that dwelleth in the secret place of the Most High Shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.
x.Darby: He that dwelleth in the secret place of the Most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.
x.KJV: He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.
x.YLT: He who is dwelling In the secret place of the Most High, In the shade of the Mighty lodgeth habitually,

nt: The psalmist is speaking as if the **Most High**, that is, God, were actually a **shelter** in which a person could live. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The one who depends on the Most High for protection]

The psalmist is using this expression as a title for God. Your language may have a comparable title that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. If you have already translated Psalm 18, see how you translated this title in [Psalms 18:13](../018/013.md). Alternate translation: [God Most High] or [the Supreme God]

The psalmist is speaking as if God actually had a **shadow**. He is using the image to represent care, the way a shadow provides a cool place to rest in hot climates. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will continually experience Shaddai’s care]
The word **Shaddai** is a name for God. If you have already translated Psalm 68, see how you translated this name in [Psalms 68:14](../068/014.md). Alternate translation: [the Almighty]

x.ASV: I will say of Jehovah, He is my refuge and my fortress; My God, in whom I trust.
x.Darby: I say of Jehovah, My refuge and my fortress; myGod, I will confide in him.
x.KJV: I will say of the Lord, He is my refuge and my fortress: my God; in him will I trust.
x.YLT: He is saying of Jehovah, `My refuge, and my bulwark, my God, I trust in Him,'

nt: אֹמַ֗ר לַֽ֭⁠יהוָה מַחְסִ֣⁠י וּ⁠מְצוּדָתִ֑⁠י אֱ֝לֹהַ֗⁠י אֶבְטַח־בּֽ⁠וֹ

The word translated **to** could indicate: (1) that the psalmist is saying this to Yahweh. You may wish to use second-person pronouns to indicate this. Alternate translation: [I will say to Yahweh, “You are my refuge and my fortress; you are my God, I trust in you”]; (2) that the psalmist is saying this about Yahweh. You may wish to use third-person pronouns to indicate this. Alternate translation: [I will say regarding Yahweh, “He is my refuge and my fortress; he is my God, I trust in him”]

The psalmist is speaking as if Yahweh were actually a **refuge** and a **fortress**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The source of my safety and my protection]

The terms **refuge** and **fortress** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be helpful for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [The one who keeps me completely safe]

x.ASV: For he will deliver thee from the snare of the fowler, And from the deadly pestilence.
x.Darby: Surely he shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler, [and] from the destructive pestilence.
x.KJV: Surely he shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler, and from the noisome pestilence.
x.YLT: For He delivereth thee from the snare of a fowler, From a calamitous pestilence.

nt: As the Introduction to this psalm discusses, the pronoun **you** is singular here and throughout the psalm because the psalmist is speaking individually to people whom he wants to encourage to trust Yahweh. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **plague**. He means plagues in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [from traps that people set for you and from deadly plagues]

The psalmist is speaking as if the individual whom he is addressing were a bird or small animal that a **trapper** was trying to catch in a **snare**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from anyone who would deceptively try to harm you]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be helpful in your language. Alternate translation: [and he will also rescue you from the plague of calamities]

The psalmist is using this possessive form to describe a **plague** that would cause **calamities**, meaning, specifically, many deaths. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from every deadly plague]

x.ASV: He will cover thee with his pinions, And under his wings shalt thou take refuge: His truth is a shield and a buckler.
x.Darby: He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou find refuge: his truth is a shield and buckler.
x.KJV: He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust: his truth shall be thy shield and buckler.
x.YLT: With His pinion He covereth thee over, And under His wings thou dost trust, A shield and buckler is His truth.

nt: These two phrases mean similar things. Translate them according to the decisions your team has made regarding translating parallelism in Hebrew poetry. Alternate translation: [He will cover you with his feathers, so you will be able to shelter under his wings] or [You will shelter under the cover of his wings]

The psalmist is speaking as if Yahweh were a bird and as if the individual he is addressing were one of its chicks. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He will protect you the way a bird protects its chicks by covering them with its wings]

The psalmist is speaking as if Yahweh’s **faithfulness** were actually a **shield** and **buckler**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [His faithfulness is dependable protection]

The word translated as **rampart** could refer to: (1) a wall around a city that would protect it from enemy attack. In that case, the psalmist would be using a shield that protected an individual soldier and a wall that protected an entire city to mean protection in general. Alternate translation: [His faithfulness is like military protection] or (2) a small shield. In that case, the psalmist would be using a large shield and a small shield together to mean all of the armor that a soldier would wear into battle. Alternate translation: [His faithfulness is like protective armor]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [He will faithfully protect you like a shield and buckler]

x.ASV: Thou shalt not be afraid for the terror by night, Nor for the arrow that flieth by day;
x.Darby: Thou shalt not be afraid for the terror by night, for the arrow that flieth by day,
x.KJV: Thou shalt not be afraid for the terror by night; nor for the arrow that flieth by day;
x.YLT: Thou art not afraid of fear by night, Of arrow that flieth by day,

nt: The psalmist is using things that might happen at **night** and during the **day** to mean things that might happen at any time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [of any dangers that might harm you at any time]

The psalmist is using this possessive form to describe something that might happen during the **night** that would cause a person to feel **terror**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [of terrifying things that might happen during the night]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be helpful in your language. Alternate translation: [and you will not be afraid of the arrow that flies by day]

The psalmist is speaking of how an **arrow … flies** without indicating that this is the result of someone shooting it from a bow. This may create the impression that an arrow is a living thing that can fly on its own. If it would be helpful in your language, you could indicate the agent who is responsible for the arrow flying. Alternate translation: [of an arrow that someone might shoot at you]

The psalmist is using one type of weapon, an **arrow**, to mean weapons in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [of any weapon that someone might use to try to harm you]

x.ASV: For the pestilence that walketh in darkness, Nor for the destruction that wasteth at noonday.
x.Darby: For the pestilence that walketh in darkness, for the destruction that wasteth at noonday.
x.KJV: Nor for the pestilence that walketh in darkness; nor for the destruction that wasteth at noonday.
x.YLT: Of pestilence in thick darkness that walketh, Of destruction that destroyeth at noon,

nt: מִ֭⁠דֶּבֶר בָּ⁠אֹ֣פֶל יַהֲלֹ֑ךְ מִ֝⁠קֶּ֗טֶב יָשׁ֥וּד צָהֳרָֽיִם

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and you will not be afraid of the plague that walks in darkness, and you will not be afraid of the destruction that wastes at midday]
מִ֭⁠דֶּבֶר בָּ⁠אֹ֣פֶל יַהֲלֹ֑ךְ מִ֝⁠קֶּ֗טֶב יָשׁ֥וּד צָהֳרָֽיִם

The psalmist is using things that might happen secretly and things that might happen openly to mean things that might happen in any way. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. It may be helpful to begin a new sentence here. Alternate translation: [You will not have to be concerned about dangers that you cannot see coming or those that you can see coming]

The psalmist is speaking of a **plague** as if it were a living thing that **walks** around. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that spreads]

The psalmist is speaking as if this plague were actually spreading from person to person **in the darkness**, meaning at night. He means that the plague spreads without people realizing it, in the same way that people do not realize what is happening in the darkness of night because they cannot see it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [invisibly]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **destruction**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [of destructive things that cause great damage]

Here, **midday**, the time when the sun is brightest in the sky, represents “openly and obviously.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in broad daylight]

x.ASV: A thousand shall fall at thy side, And ten thousand at thy right hand; But it shall not come nigh thee.
x.Darby: A thousand shall fall at thy side, and ten thousand at thy right hand; [but] it shall not come nigh thee.
x.KJV: A thousand shall fall at thy side, and ten thousand at thy right hand; but it shall not come nigh thee.
x.YLT: There fall at thy side a thousand, And a myriad at thy right hand, Unto thee it cometh not nigh.

nt: יִפֹּ֤ל מִ⁠צִּדְּ⁠ךָ֨ ׀ אֶ֗לֶף וּ⁠רְבָבָ֥ה מִ⁠ימִינֶ֑⁠ךָ אֵ֝לֶ֗י⁠ךָ לֹ֣א יִגָּֽשׁ

The psalmist is using a hypothetical situation to help his listeners appreciate how confidently they can trust God to protect them. Use the natural form in your language for expressing a hypothetical situation. Alternate translation: [Suppose a thousand fell at your side. Suppose a myriad fell at your right hand. Even then, it would not approach toward you]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [A thousand may fall at your side, and a myriad may fall at your right hand]

The psalmist is using the term **fall** to mean “die,” since people typically fall down when they die. Be sure that it is clear in your translation that he is not referring to people falling down accidentally. Alternate translation: [A thousand may die at your side, and a myriad may die at your right hand]

The pronoun **it** refers to any deadly danger such as the psalmist has described in verses 5 and 6. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [no deadly dangerous thing will approach toward you]

Since the psalmist says that people may die right next to and all around the individual whom he is addressing, he does not mean that danger will actually **not** even **approach** that individual. Rather, he is using this expression as an overstatement to mean that dangerous things will not kill him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [no deadly dangerous thing will kill you]

x.ASV: Only with thine eyes shalt thou behold, And see the reward of the wicked.
x.Darby: Only with thine eyes shalt thou behold, and see the reward of the wicked.
x.KJV: Only with thine eyes shalt thou behold and see the reward of the wicked.
x.YLT: But with thine eyes thou lookest, And the reward of the wicked thou seest,

nt: It might seem that the expression **observe with your eyes** contains extra information that would be unnatural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [observe]

The psalmist is using this possessive form to describe the **wicked** receiving a **recompense**, not the wicked giving a recompense to someone. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and see the wicked receiving their recompense]

The psalmist is speaking as if God were actually repaying the wicked an amount that was due to them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and see God paying the wicked back for what they have done] or [and see God punishing the wicked]

The psalmist is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [wicked people]

x.Darby: Because thou hast made Jehovah, my refuge, the Most High, thy dwelling-place,
x.KJV: Because thou hast made the Lord, which is my refuge, even the most High, thy habitation;
x.YLT: (For Thou, O Jehovah, art my refuge,) The Most High thou madest thy habitation.

The psalmist is speaking as if Yahweh were actually a **refuge** in which a person could take shelter and a **dwelling** in which a person could live. See how you translated the expression “dwelling in the shelter” in [91:1](../091/001.md) and the expression “My refuge” in [91:2](../091/002.md). Alternate translation: [you are depending on Yahweh, the source of my safety, the Most High, for your protection]

x.ASV: There shall no evil befall thee, Neither shall any plague come nigh thy tent.
x.Darby: There shall no evil befall thee, neither shall any plague come nigh thy tent.
x.KJV: There shall no evil befall thee, neither shall any plague come nigh thy dwelling.
x.YLT: Evil happeneth not unto thee, And a plague cometh not near thy tent,

nt: לֹֽא־תְאֻנֶּ֣ה אֵלֶ֣י⁠ךָ רָעָ֑ה וְ֝⁠נֶ֗גַע לֹא־יִקְרַ֥ב בְּ⁠אָהֳלֶֽ⁠ךָ

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The first phrase states the general idea, and then the second phrase gives a specific example. Translate these phrases according to the decisions your team has made regarding translating parallelism in Hebrew poetry. Alternate translation: [evil will not happen to you; no, a plague will not come near to your tent] or [bad things will not happen to you where you live]
לֹֽא־תְאֻנֶּ֣ה אֵלֶ֣י⁠ךָ רָעָ֑ה וְ֝⁠נֶ֗גַע לֹא־יִקְרַ֥ב בְּ⁠אָהֳלֶֽ⁠ךָ

The psalmist is speaking of how **evil will not happen** and **a plague will not come near** without indicating that these are the results of Yahweh’s actions on behalf of those who trust in him. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate Yahweh’s agency explicitly here. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will prevent evil from happening to you; yes, he will keep plagues from coming near to your tent]
The psalmist is using one kind of home, a **tent**, to mean all kinds of homes. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your home]

x.ASV: For he will give his angels charge over thee, To keep thee in all thy ways.
x.Darby: For he shall give his angels charge concerning thee, to keep thee in all thy ways:
x.KJV: For he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways.
x.YLT: For His messengers He chargeth for thee, To keep thee in all thy ways,

nt: The pronoun **he** refers to God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [God will command]

The psalmist is speaking of the activities of the individual he is addressing as if they were **ways** or paths that the individual was walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in all of your activities]

x.ASV: They shall bear thee up in their hands, Lest thou dash thy foot against a stone.
x.Darby: They shall bear thee up in [their] hands, lest thou dash thy foot against a stone.
x.KJV: They shall bear thee up in their hands, lest thou dash thy foot against a stone.
x.YLT: On the hands they bear thee up, Lest thou smite against a stone thy foot.

nt: The psalmist is using one harmful thing that might happen to a person, hitting his **foot** against a **stone**, to mean every kind of harmful thing that might happen to a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [so that harmful things do not happen to you]

The psalmist is using the word translated as **lest** to introduce an outcome that he does not want to happen. Because of this, he first reassures the person he is addressing that God’s angels will protect him so that this will not happen. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that avoiding this outcome is the purpose of the instruction. Alternate translation: [Otherwise, you might hit your foot against a stone] or [Otherwise, harmful things might happen to you]

x.ASV: Thou shalt tread upon the lion and adder: The young lion and the serpent shalt thou trample under foot.
x.Darby: Thou shalt tread upon the lion and the adder; the young lion and the dragon shalt thou trample under foot.
x.KJV: Thou shalt tread upon the lion and adder: the young lion and the dragon shalt thou trample under feet.
x.YLT: On lion and asp thou treadest, Thou trampest young lion and dragon.

nt: עַל־שַׁ֣חַל וָ⁠פֶ֣תֶן תִּדְרֹ֑ךְ תִּרְמֹ֖ס כְּפִ֣יר וְ⁠תַנִּֽין

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **lion**, **adder**, **young lion**, or **serpent**. He means such animals in general. It may be more natural in your language to express this meaning by using plural forms. Alternate translation: [You will tread on lions and adders; you will trample young lions and serpents]
עַל־שַׁ֣חַל וָ⁠פֶ֣תֶן תִּדְרֹ֑ךְ תִּרְמֹ֖ס כְּפִ֣יר וְ⁠תַנִּֽין

The psalmist may be using the terms **tread** and **trample** to mean “defeat.” People in this culture would force defeated enemies to lie down and then place a foot on top of them to show how completely they had defeated them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You will defeat any lion or adder that attacks you; yes, you will defeat any young lion or serpent that attacks you]
עַל־שַׁ֣חַל וָ⁠פֶ֣תֶן תִּדְרֹ֑ךְ תִּרְמֹ֖ס כְּפִ֣יר וְ⁠תַנִּֽין

The psalmist is using a hypothetical situation to help the individual he is addressing appreciate how Yahweh will protect him. Use a natural form in your language for expressing a hypothetical situation. To do that, it may be helpful to combine the two parallel phrases in this verse. Alternate translation: [Suppose a lion or a snake attacks you. Yahweh will enable you to defeat it, and it will not harm you] or [If a lion or a snake attacks you, you will defeat it and it will not harm you]

nt: This is the beginning of a direct quotation from Yahweh. You may wish to indicate that in your translation, using a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says, “Because he clings to me”]

The psalmist assumes that his listeners will know that by **cling**, he means to cling to someone out of love and devotion. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [he is devoted to me]

The word **name** could refer to: (1) Yahweh as a person, since each person has a name. Alternate translation: [he knows me personally]; (2) Yahweh’s reputation, which reflects his character. Alternate translation: [he knows my character and so trusts me]
